---
title: "Pain is not a damage report"
description: "A reading journey for hands-on practitioners: what pain actually is, how loosely it tracks the tissue, and what that changes in the room."
---

::: {.part}
Start here
:::

::: {.stand}
Almost everyone who comes to you is in pain, and almost everyone arrives with the same
model of it: something in there is broken, the amount it hurts tells you how broken, and
the job is to find the break and fix it.

That model is wrong in a specific and useful way. Not wrong as in *the pain is imaginary*
— it is as real as anything gets. Wrong as in *the dial is not connected to the thing
you think it is connected to*.
:::

This is a reading journey through what is established about that, in eleven short stops and
about half an hour. Every figure can be operated. Every claim names its source before you
meet it, and says how much that source can carry.

We wrote it for people who work with bodies and hands — massage therapists, bodyworkers,
physiotherapists, nurses, movement and somatic practitioners — and for one situation in
particular: the client who has been told their scan looks terrible, and believes it.

::: {.ab}
[Who it is for]{.lbl}

You do not need a science background. Where a technical word is genuinely the right one
we introduce it, link it, and say what it means in ordinary language beside it.

You are also likely to have been taught some of this already, possibly in paid training,
possibly with great confidence, and possibly in a version the research has since moved
on from. We have tried to be careful about that. Where something is well established we
say so plainly; where it is thin we say that too, and there is a whole part at the end
about the claims on this page that cannot carry the weight people put on them.
:::

::: {.ab}
[What is here]{.lbl}

**One · what pain is.** How much of it there is, why an experience is not a reading, and
what happens to a signal on its way in.

**Two · how loose the link is.** What a scan of a pain-free back actually looks like, and
what a coloured light does to a fixed physical stimulus.

**Three · when pain stays.** How a nervous system turns its own gain up, and how much of
a treatment is the room rather than the technique.

**Four · being honest about it.** What teaching people about pain measurably does, which
is less than the field would like, and how much weight each thing on this page can bear.
:::

Nothing here is medical advice, and nothing here is a protocol. It is a record of what
two readers found in the literature, written down in the order it made sense.

::: {.hands}
[Before you start]{.t}
If you take one thing from this, we would rather it were this: **hurt and harm are
different quantities.** A great deal of what follows is that sentence, with the evidence
attached.
:::
